routes.name: Liberty Crack
routes.fa: Steve Marts, Don McPherson & Fred Stanley, July 1965
gear: double rack of cams to 3 inches, with a second set of small/finger-size cams (aliens or equivalent) through #3
aid gear for C2 (or a 5.11-5.13 free rack)
hazards: Sustained steep climbing high on the east face with serious exposure
The Lithuanian Lip roof and thin crux pitches demand confident hard climbing or clean aid
Afternoon thunderstorms on the fully exposed face
Rockfall onto the lower pitches from parties and the gully above
routes.overview: Liberty Crack is the most celebrated route on Liberty Bell and #24 in Roper & Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America, splitting the steep, 1,200-foot east face with a soaring line of cracks. The signature roof on Pitch 2, the Lithuanian Roof, is named for Alex Bertulis' Lithuanian heritage — he made an unsuccessful attempt on the roof in 1964 with Steve Marts before Marts, Don McPherson, and Fred Stanley completed the route the following year. Most parties fix and aid the crux Pitches 2-3 (or free them at 5.11-5.13-) and climb the remaining pitches free before topping out on the Beckey Route's final slab.
routes.beta: A 12-pitch, Grade V east-face route that accommodates full aid, hybrid, or free climbing styles. Most parties take two days, often fixing the first three pitches and returning the next day to climb to the summit.
routes.turnaround: Judge progress by the lower pitches; if you are slow reaching the Lithuanian Lip or weather builds, retreat by rappel before committing high on the steep face.
routes.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
routes.descent: Rappel the Liberty Bell descent route (Beckey Route side) from the summit: two rappels of about 25 m, which a single 60 m rope handles.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout (east of Washington Pass)
waypoints.directions: Park in the pullout on the north side of SR-20 at the hairpin curve, roughly 0.3 to 0.5 mile past the Washington Pass Overlook turnoff and a short distance east of Washington Pass. SR-20 is gated for the winter and typically doesn't reopen until mid-to-late April or early May, so this approach isn't accessible until the highway opens for the season.

waypoints.name: Base of east face
waypoints.directions: Walk back west along the SR-20 shoulder toward the pass to the small pond on the south side of the highway, skirt the pond's east end, and pick up the cairned boot path heading north into the timber. It climbs steeply through forest for 15-20 minutes before breaking out onto talus directly beneath the East Face; the cairns are genuinely hard to follow before dawn, and there is no water between the car and the wall.

waypoints.name: Liberty Bell Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: From the talus, pick the line by the huge roof above you — the Lithuanian Lip — with Liberty Crack the continuous crack passing to its right; do not scramble straight up the fall line beneath it, which lands parties on the neighbouring East Face routes. The standard entry traverses in from the left for roughly 40 feet on third- and fourth-class ledges to the ledges under the true first-pitch crack, and twelve pitches then lead to the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder.

sectionBreakdown.note: Pre-dawn approach from the SR-20 hairpin pullout; some parties bivy at the base the night before to start at first light. Climb all 12 pitches, then rappel the two-rappel Beckey-side descent…
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Big single day (some bivy at base)

routes.detailed_rack: A double rack of cams from tips to 3 inches, a full set of nuts, plus a small selection of aid gear (offset nuts, cam hooks) if climbing the Lithuanian Lip at C2; or a thin free rack if attempting the 5.11 free climbing. Two ropes if fixing the lower pitches or rappelling the East Face; the standard notch descent needs only one.
pro_tips: Be solid at the grade you choose, whether 5.11 free or C2 aid
Start at first light for the twelve-pitch day
Fix the Lithuanian Lip strategy in advance
Watch the weather; the east face is fully exposed
watch_out: Rope snags on the steep descent rappels
routes.pro_needs: Protection is excellent in the splitter cracks, with the crux being either the hard free climbing or the clean aid through the roof. Bring enough to protect sustained, steep terrain over many pitches.
routes.best_season: Mid-July through September on warm, dry granite.
routes.approach: Liberty Crack climbs the East Face, and its approach does NOT start from the Blue Lake Trailhead — that's the trailhead for the west-side Beckey Route. Instead, drive to the pullout on the north side of SR-20 at the hairpin curve a short distance east of Washington Pass (about 0.3-0.5 mile past the Washington Pass Overlook turnoff). Park there and walk back (west) along the road shoulder to a small pond on the south side of the highway. Skirt the pond's east end and pick up a boot path — cairned but easy to lose in the dark on an alpine start — heading north into the forest. The path climbs steeply through timber for 15-20 minutes before breaking out onto talus/boulder terrain directly beneath the East Face, about an hour from the car. There is no reliable water on this short approach, so fill up before leaving the car. The main hazards are losing the cairned track in the trees pre-dawn and loose talus/scree footing at the base.
routes.descent_text:
The standard way off is the two-rappel Beckey-side descent, shared with Liberty Crack (Free), Freedom Rider and the Beckey Route. From the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder where the last pitch ends, traverse third-class ledges climber's left to the double-bolt station - the final few metres to it are exposed - and make the first rappel, under 30 m, down toward Beckey Gully. Do not link this into one double-length rappel to the notch: that variation has a poor reputation for jammed ropes. A second rappel of roughly the same length reaches Beckey Gully and the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch, and from there you downclimb and hike the scree and boulder gully below the notch - snow-covered or loose and unpleasant depending on the season - to the climbers' trail and the Blue Lake Trail. Manage the ropes carefully on both: the terrain is steep and snags are the common problem here.

Plan the walk back before you start down. Liberty Crack parties park at the East Face pullout on SR-20 rather than at the Blue Lake Trailhead, so this descent puts you down on the far side of the mountain from the car, meaning either a shuttle or roughly a mile back along the highway shoulder. A rappel line down the east face that returns you directly to your packs at the base of the route has been reported - a bolted line of six stations on the right side of the wall, where a single 60 m rope reaches each station but is tight at a couple of them, so parties carry a second rope or plan a short downclimb. The four-rappel line off M&M Ledge is a real descent, but it belongs to Thin Red Line rather than to this route; do not plan on it here.
routes.bail: Retreat by rappel is feasible from the lower pitches but grows committing above the Lithuanian Lip; commit to the climb only with confidence and good weather.

pitch_detail.notes: A right-facing corner then a splitter crack lead straight up to a clean bolted belay shortly below the Lithuanian Lip; some parties aid/hybrid this pitch.

The historic Lithuanian Lip: go up and out the roof, get over the top, then aid a bolt ladder (or free climb it at 5.13- for strong parties) to a bolted belay. Most parties aid this section for the route's standard 5.11a grade.
Face climbing or aid with fixed heads leads to a crack and old pitons, ending at a bolted anchor; freeing is fastest from here upward.
Jam a nice crack that hardens from 5.8 to 5.10 as it goes, ending at another bolted belay.
Continue upward along a corner system to another bolted belay; a relatively relaxed pitch between harder sections.
Mostly easy stemming (mind loose rock) leads to a brief crux surmounting a big block, protected by a single shiny bolt, to bolted anchors.
Steep moves off the belay gain a ramp/corner with a long-runner bolt and 5.10- moves over an overlap to a decent seat; belay is built from pitons and small cams.
Go up and left through fun quartz features then 5.6 chimneys to a triangular ledge with a finger-crack gear anchor.
A long, excellent pitch up a left-facing corner and slab with beautiful moments of exposure over the East Face; belay off a large tree.
Continue up easy terrain until reaching sandy ledges; a rappel anchor is available nearby in case a party strays onto the wrong terrain.
Third-class ledges allow unroping or simul-climbing toward the summit shoulder alcove.
Easy terrain leads to the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder, the start of the standard two-rappel descent into Beckey Gully shared with Liberty Crack (Free), Freedom Rider, and the Beckey Route.

days.note: Pre-dawn approach from the SR-20 hairpin pullout; climb the 12-pitch aid/free line, then rappel the standard two-rappel Beckey-side descent. Documented ascents run 9-10 hrs car-to-car for fit parties; some bivy at the base for an easier pre-dawn start.

access.fees: No climbing permit; NW Forest Pass $5 (day) or $30 (annual)
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (outside North Cascades National Park boundary)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (Blue Lakes Trailhead, 1 mile west of Washington Pass)

overnight_permit.where: Outside any wilderness boundary; parties bivy informally at the Blue Lake Trailhead lot or the highway hairpin pullout east of the pass. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is needed to park, and no camping is allowed within a quarter mile of Blue Lake itself.

road.name: WA-20 hairpin pullout east of Washington Pass (East Face climbers' trail)
road.status: A paved-highway pullout on a hairpin curve on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass; like the Blue Lake TH this is roadside parking directly off pavement, no dirt-road driving required.
road.driveNote: About 3-3.5 hours from Seattle via I-5 to Burlington then east on SR-20, or via US-2/US-97 through Wenatchee and north on SR-153/SR-20 from the east.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam/Diablo area and Silver Star/Mazama, typically early-to-mid December through late April or early May depending on snowpack, making this pullout unreachable by car in winter/spring.

climate.typical: Steep east-facing granite; warm dry summer days with afternoon convection.

bySeason.summer: Prime; warm dry granite, afternoon storm risk

emergency.notes: No reliable cell coverage; carry a satellite communicator. Use 911 for emergencies.
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster / Confluence Health, Wenatchee

crowds.peakTraffic: Summer weekends, especially among parties attempting the free ascent or the classic aid line
crowds.estimatePerSeason: A Fifty Classic Climb with strong reputation and steady traffic, but the sustained 5.11a/C2 grade filters out casual climbers; expect a handful of parties on route on a given weekend rather than the stacked queues seen on the Beckey Route

fitnessSpec.hiking: Short, steep forest and talus approach from the SR-20 hairpin to the east face base
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Aid rack or full trad rack plus aiders if aiding, roughly 20-25 lb

partner_requirements.approachTime: Roughly 1 hour from the SR-20 hairpin pullout to the base of the east face
requiredSkills: 5.10-5.11 crack/face leading or C2 aid climbing
big-wall-style rope and gear management across 12 pitches
efficient multi-pitch transitions to beat afternoon storms
route-finding on a sustained, complex east face
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced grade IV multi-pitch leader; confident free climbing 5.10+ or comfortable aid/French-freeing thin seams; needs stamina and composure for a full 12-pitch alpine day

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September on warm, dry granite

June.reason: Base and lower pitches can still be damp or snow-affected; not reliably in condition

October.reason: Early snow and cold possible; highway may still be open but conditions unreliable for a long committing route

September.reason: Cooler but stable, with fewer parties on route

weather.typical: Steep east-facing granite with warm dry summer days
weather.probability: Afternoon convection is common; getting caught high on the fully exposed face in a storm is a serious hazard

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence - sustained steep climbing with serious exposure high on the face, the Lithuanian Lip crux, and a long, complex rappel descent with rockfall risk from parties and terrain above

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer rock route; the east face and its talus approach are not an avalanche path during the July-September season

rappel_detail.pull: Under 30m, single 60m rope. Do not link this into one double-length rappel to the notch — that variation has a poor reputation for jammed ropes.
rappel_detail.notes: After topping out, traverse third-class ledges climber's left to a bolted anchor in an alcove; first rappel down toward Beckey Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor (double-bolt station in an alcove near the topout)
hazards: the last few metres to the anchor cross an exposed sloping ledge
the station is genuinely hard to spot from above and parties have rappelled past the line or had to climb back up to find it; note it before you commit to going down
rappel_detail.station: Reached by traversing climber's left along the third-class ledges at the top of the route, or by downclimbing the last pitch of the Beckey Route. The anchor is shiny bolts with chains set in a corner or shallow alcove on a steep wall overlooking the Liberty Bell-Concord notch — you have to look down over the edge a little to see it, and it is not visible from the ledge above.

rappel_detail.pull: About 25m, single 60m rope reaches the notch.
rappel_detail.notes: Second rappel reaches Beckey Gully / the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch; from there downclimb/hike the gully to the climbers' trail.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor (the second station is also described as a tree — judge what is there)
hazards: this last rappel is the one repeatedly reported for stuck ropes, in more than one case costing a party a re-lead of an adjacent route to recover the strand

you are rappelling over a climbing route and above a busy approach gully, so both your rope and anything you knock loose land on other parties — the notch echoes badly enough that shouted communication is unreliable when it is busy
the notch below is snow early or loose scree later, and the gully leading down from it sheds rock readily
rappel_detail.station: A second set of bolts and chains, described as sitting in an alcove with a tree beside it, dropping directly into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.

routes.rappel_count_note: Standard/primary Liberty Crack descent, consistently described: two rappels of roughly 25-30m on bolted anchors down to Beckey Gully/the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then hike down the gully. It is the same descent as for Liberty Crack (Free). The four-rap M&M Ledge/East-Face line is real but belongs to Thin Red Line.

approach_variants.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
approach_variants.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is not approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the west side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Some parties instead rappel the East Face to return directly to their packs.
hazards: loose talus and boulders at the base of the wall
cairned forest path is genuinely hard to follow before dawn
no water between the car and the wall
rockfall from parties on the East Face routes above
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the talus, Liberty Crack is the obvious continuous vertical crack that passes to the right of the huge roof high on the wall — the roof is the Lithuanian Lip, and it is the single feature that identifies the line even in flat light. Do not scramble straight up beneath it. The standard entry traverses in from the left for roughly 40 feet on third- and fourth-class ledges to reach the ledges directly under the true first-pitch crack; there is also a fourth-class alternative that goes up the right-hand side of the block at the base. Parties that head straight up the fall line from the talus end up on the neighbouring East Face lines rather than on Liberty Crack — the East Face here holds a whole cluster of routes within a few rope lengths of each other, so pick the line by the roof above you, not by whichever crack is nearest.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.
approach_variants.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
hazards: deep moat between snow and rock at the base of the wall
hard refrozen snow over talus — a slip runs out badly
SR-20 is gated all winter, so this window only opens once the highway reopens (typically mid-late April to early May)
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identifier is still the big roof — Liberty Crack is the continuous crack running past the right side of the Lithuanian Lip. What changes is the last few metres: a deep moat opens where the snow pulls away from the base of the wall, and getting from snow into the rock can mean a committing step across or a short stemming move down and back up out of the gap. Scout along the base rather than dropping into the first moat you meet; parties have found the moat mellowing out within about thirty feet of where they first reached it.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

areas.name: Palisade Head
areas.approach: Routes in the amphitheater are best reached by abseiling in from the top; routes from Danger High Voltage southward can be reached from the talus by descending Southern Escape Gully. Walking the talus under the cliff is simple in decent weather, but storms, freezing conditions and lake surf can block it entirely, and a boulder cave near the amphitheater's south edge adds low fifth-class climbing where a rope is wise.

areas.name: Liberty Bell Mountain
areas.blurb: Liberty Bell Mountain (7,720 ft summit; some older USGS-derived listings round to 7,745-7,750 ft) is the northernmost spire of the Liberty Bell Group in Washington's North Cascades, about one mile south of Washington Pass on SR-20 (North Cascades Highway), straddling the Chelan-Okanogan county line. Built of granite from the Golden Horn batholith, it offers high-quality alpine rock with an unusually short approach (roughly 1.5-2.5 hours from the Blue Lake Trailhead) — from the classic Grade II 5.6 Beckey Route on the southwest face to the big east-face lines Liberty Crack, Independence Route, and Thin Red Line, all first climbed as aid routes in the 1960s and since substantially freed. First ascent September 27, 1946, by Fred Beckey, Jerry O'Neil, and Charles Welsh via the southwest face. Managed by the Methow Valley Ranger District of the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency Pass is required to park at the Blue Lake Trailhead, though no climbing permit is needed. SR-20 closes for winter (typically Nov-May), cutting off vehicle access.

areas.name: Summit Chief Mountain
areas.blurb: Highest of the 'Chief' cluster (with Middle Chief, 7,120', and Little Big Chief, 7,225') anchoring the divide between the Waptus and Cooper/Pete Lake drainages deep in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Sits on the King-Kittitas county line about 9 miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass, with Chimney Rock (its line parent) immediately southwest across the connecting ridge. First climbed in 1925; the standard line is a long approach-then-scramble up the Southeast Face.
